Lucius, his mother's name for the half-built birdhouse they had started when he was nine, still sat on the ledge, its roof missing. She teased him about it while he loaded the car: a future engineer who could not finish four walls and a perch. He laughed, and she laughed louder, listing every project he had abandoned, the kite, the radio, the tiled step. Then she picked up the birdhouse and turned it over in her hands. Underneath, in pencil, were the measurements for the roof, written in his childish script and never used. She stopped talking. She set the birdhouse back on the ledge very carefully, as if it might break, and told him she would leave it exactly as it was until he came home to finish it.

Larissa, who had not set foot in a church in ten years, watched Father Bruno try to arrange one long table for two groups that had never eaten together: the women who kept the old saint's-day customs and the newer members who kept none. He fussed over place cards, shifting names, and Larissa found it absurd, almost comic, that a priest should worry so much about seating. She whispered as much to the woman beside her. Then she noticed what he was doing. He had placed each older weaver beside a newer one whose pattern she had once criticized, and on every plate he had folded a scrap of the other's cloth. g.passage:
I pinned the sheets on Silas's line that spring,
the Cornish wind half wrestling them from me,
and laughed to think how many years we'd spent
at chess-club boards, two old men keeping score
of every bishop lost, each petty win.
He'd beaten me at last the week before.
I meant to tease him over it today.
But in his drawer, beneath the clothespin tin,
I found a notebook of my games, not his,
each losing move of mine marked out in ink
and next to it, in his small careful hand,
the better move, and then: "Show Mabel this."
He never had. The wind went still. I stood
with one white sheet held open in my arms
and folded it as if it were a flag.

ZEYNEP: (holding up a pocket watch) Your grandfather wound this every morning for forty years. And now you want to say goodbye to him with a speech?
APONI: A short one. Something proper. People expect it.
ZEYNEP: People expect sandwiches, too. (She snaps the watch open, grinning.) He'd have fallen asleep by your second sentence.
APONI: (laughing despite himself) He fell asleep at my graduation.
ZEYNEP: Twice. (Her grin fades. She listens to the watch, which has stopped.) He brought it here the week before he died. Asked me to fix it. I told him there was no hurry.
APONI: There wasn't.
ZEYNEP: (quietly, setting the watch on the counter between them) There was. I just didn't hear it. Wind it, child. Not for the speech. Let it run on the plateau a little longer than he did.

I had spent a month dreading the afternoon Dwayne's aunt Kemoy would join our wedding planning at the salt-water pool in Port of Spain, where my mother and I did our best thinking with our feet in the water. Kemoy had opinions, everyone warned me, and she had opposed the engagement. I rehearsed polite refusals. When she arrived, she criticized the guest list, the menu, the color of the tablecloths, and I felt my mother stiffen beside me. Then Kemoy pulled a folded paper from her bag: the name of a caterer who owed her a favor, a cousin with a free hall, a band that played for half price. She had not come to oppose us. g.passage:
"Wrong door again," I muttered, finding your envelope in my dryer at the laundromat this morning.
Dear Talon,
I am writing because this is the third letter of yours that has landed in my machine, my mailbox, or my coat pocket, and I am beginning to suspect the wall between our apartments is thinner than either of us thought. I was ready to slide it under your door with a stern note. I even drafted the note. But the envelope had come open in the wash, and I read the first line before I could stop myself. It was from the hospital, about your sister. I am sorry I read it. I am more sorry that you have been carrying this alone on the other side of a wall I complain about every night. My door is open after six. I will bring the coffee, and I will not mention the mail.
Tallulah

g.passage: Four duties came with my summer job at the rural post office outside Naples: sort the mail, sell the stamps, lock the safe, and give directions to anyone who wandered down from the hills. I was proud of the fourth. So when a hiker named Matteo stumbled in at dusk, sunburned and lost, I drew him a confident map to the trailhead. An hour later Chiara, the park ranger, brought him back. My map had sent him up the wrong ridge. I expected her to tell him whose fault it was. Instead, she told him the trail signs had been moved by the wind, which was not quite true, and she asked me for a glass of water for him. After he left, she sat with me and redrew the map, slowly, landmark by landmark. I have kept that second map, folded in a drawer, for twenty years.

g.passage: Once, when I was eleven, I asked my father why he had left Japan, and Shigeru only handed me a knife and an onion. That was the beginning of our agreement. In the galley of the fishing boat he cooked for, docked each winter in Hokkaido's colder harbors, we talked in English about everything else: the crew's appetites, the price of squid, my school in Seattle. I translated menus and invoices for him. He taught me to fillet a fish in four strokes. Neither of us mentioned the subject. Then, the winter I turned seventeen, a deckhand asked him the same question I had asked. My father answered in Japanese, at length, while I stood at the cutting board pretending not to understand. I understood every word. That night, Sachiko, he said, you can ask me again. I did not, and I have never been sure whether that silence was kindness or cowardice.

g.explanation: 앞부분에서 Eulalio는 장학금을 포기한 일을 오랫동안 누나 Valentina 탓으로 여겨 왔다. 밑줄 문장은 어머니가 스스로 말할 수 없어 딸에게 대신 말하게 했다는 사실을 밝혀, 그 원망의 대상이 잘못되었음을 드러낸다. 이후 Eulalio가 팔짱을 풀고 계속 읽어 달라고 하는 반응도 이를 뒷받침하므로 B가 정답이다. A는 어머니가 혼자 노점을 운영했다는 내용과 맞지 않고, C는 편지를 지어냈다는 근거가 없으며, D는 편지의 일상적 내용을 설명하는 문장이 아니다.

seed.topicSeed: a quiet library in Hanoi; a stepfather and his stepdaughter while deciding whether a rule still applies

g.passage: After my mother remarried, Anh became the keeper of one rule in our house: no talking in the reading room of the old library in Hanoi, where he took me every Sunday. I resented it. For a year we sat across from each other in silence, he with his newspapers and I, Putri, with whatever novel I could pretend to read. I decided the rule was his way of avoiding me. Then, the week before I left for university, I asked whether the rule still applied now that I was grown. He thought about it, then slid a library slip across the table. On it he had written, in pencil, the title of every book I had read there that year, with a small mark beside the ones I had finished twice. __He had been paying attention the entire time.__ We walked home talking, loudly, the whole way.
g.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It confirms the narrator's early belief that the stepfather avoided her.
It explains why the library enforced strict silence in its reading room.
It states the realization that overturns the narrator's view of the rule.
It introduces a new rule that replaces the one the stepfather once kept firmly.
g.explanation: 화자는 침묵 규칙을 의붓아버지 Anh이 자신을 피하는 방식이라고 여겼다. 그러나 그가 화자가 1년 동안 읽은 모든 책과 두 번 읽은 책까지 적어 둔 쪽지를 내밀자, 밑줄 문장은 그가 내내 관심을 기울이고 있었다는 깨달음을 직접 말한다. 이 깨달음이 규칙에 대한 화자의 기존 해석을 뒤집으므로 C가 정답이다. A는 반대 내용이고, B는 도서관의 정책을 설명하지 않으며, D는 새로운 규칙이 소개되지 않는다.

seed.relationship: a nurse and her night patient

seed.topicSeed: a stone bridge in Haifa; a nurse and her night patient over a decision made without asking

g.passage: I worked nights at a small clinic near the old stone bridge in Haifa, and Yitzhak was the patient who never slept. He talked instead, mostly about the bridge, which he had crossed every morning for fifty years on his way to the docks. One night his son phoned to say the family had decided to move him to a care home in another city. No one had asked him. I knew because I had been asked to keep it quiet until the papers were signed. I, Chana, said nothing, and for three nights I let him talk about the bridge as if he would walk it again. __On the fourth night I wheeled him to the window and told him.__ He was quiet a long time. Then he asked me to describe the bridge to him in the morning light, so he would have a newer picture to take with him.
g.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It introduces the bridge as a place the patient has never seen before.
It shows the narrator following the family's request to delay the news.
It marks the moment when the patient finally learns to sleep through the night.
It marks the narrator's decision to end her silence about the family's choice.
g.explanation: 화자 Chana는 가족이 Yitzhak에게 묻지 않고 요양원 이전을 결정했다는 사실을 서류 서명 전까지 숨기라는 부탁을 받고 사흘 동안 침묵한다. 밑줄 문장은 넷째 날 밤 그녀가 그 침묵을 깨고 사실을 알리는 순간을 보여 준다. 이후 Yitzhak이 다리를 묘사해 달라고 부탁하는 결말도 이 결정에서 이어지므로 D가 정답이다. A는 그가 다리를 50년간 건넜다는 내용과 맞지 않고, B는 부탁을 어기는 장면이므로 반대이며, C는 잠에 관한 변화가 나오지 않는다.

seed.relationship: a daughter and her absent father's friend
seed.conflict: about teaching a skill that is dying out
seed.topicSeed: an old cinema projection booth in Vermont; a daughter and her absent father's friend about teaching a skill that is dying out

g.passage: Efua had expected the projection booth to smell of dust, but it smelled of oil and warm metal, the way her father's hands once had. Ayesha, who had run the projectors at the small Vermont cinema with him for thirty years, threaded the film without looking, talking the whole time. Most people thought the work was finished, she said; the big theaters had gone digital, and no one needed to know how to splice a broken reel. Efua watched her fingers. They were swollen at the knuckles and moved more slowly than her voice, yet they never missed a sprocket. When the film caught, Ayesha did not curse. She simply stopped the machine, cut the damaged frame, and joined the ends with a patience that seemed almost tender. Efua realized she had come for her father's stories and was staying for this woman's hands.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Ayesha?
options: Pity for Ayesha's aging hands mixed with doubt about her skill
Growing admiration for Ayesha's careful, unhurried craftsmanship
Polite indifference toward Ayesha's work and her stories of the past
Mild irritation at Ayesha's constant talk during the screening
g.explanation: 서술자는 Ayesha의 손가락이 관절이 부어 느려졌지만 톱니 구멍을 한 번도 놓치지 않는다고 묘사한다. 필름이 걸렸을 때도 욕하지 않고 손상된 프레임을 잘라 다정하다 싶을 만큼 참을성 있게 잇는 장면을 세밀히 관찰하고, Efua는 이 여인의 손 때문에 머물게 되었다고 깨닫는다. 따라서 신중하고 서두르지 않는 기술에 대한 점점 커지는 감탄인 B가 정답이다. A는 실력에 대한 의심이 없고, C는 세밀한 관찰과 맞지 않으며, D는 그녀의 말에 대한 짜증이 드러나지 않는다.
